\chapter{And, But, Or}
\label{ch:te-and-but-or}
\hlchaptermodality{74}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can join two Telugu words or two Telugu clauses, and I can ask why and answer it.}

Complete TE-C74-because and demonstrate the chapter promise.

\section[mariyu]{\te{మరియు} (mariyu) — and}

\label{lesson:TE-C74-and}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{vagaru} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \te{మరియు}}
\textbf{\te{మరియు}} (\emph{mariyu}) — \textquotedblleft{}and\textquotedblright{}.

Telugu's everyday speech often joins two things by simply saying them one after the other, or by hanging a small \textbf{-\te{ఉ}} on the end of each. \te{మరియు} is the written, spoken-carefully form, and it is the one a list on a page will use.

Put it between two nouns you already have: \textbf{\te{నీళ్ళు} \te{మరియు} \te{పాలు}} — \textquotedblleft{}water and milk\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The first way you have had to put two things in one sentence.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{mariyu}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{mariyu}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} join two words you know with \emph{mariyu}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{dayacēsi}, then say \emph{mariyu}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \te{మరియు} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}and\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[kānī]{\te{కానీ} (kānī) — but}

\label{lesson:TE-C74-but}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{mariyu} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \te{కానీ}}
\textbf{\te{కానీ}} (\emph{kānī}) — \textquotedblleft{}but\textquotedblright{}.

\te{కానీ} turns a sentence around. Where \te{మరియు} adds, \te{కానీ} takes back: it warns the listener that what comes next does not match what came before.

\textbf{\te{నాకు} \te{టీ} \te{ఇష్టం}, \te{కానీ} \te{పాలు} \te{వద్దు}} — \textquotedblleft{}I like tea, but no milk.\textquotedblright{} This one word is what lets you disagree politely instead of only saying \te{లేదు}.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Two clauses, and a way to set the second against the first.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{kānī}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{kānī}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} say something you like, then \emph{kānī}, then something about it you do not
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{kṣamin̄caṇḍi}, then say \emph{kānī}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \te{కానీ} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}but\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[lēdā]{\te{లేదా} (lēdā) — or}

\label{lesson:TE-C74-or}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{kānī} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \te{లేదా}}
\textbf{\te{లేదా}} (\emph{lēdā}) — \textquotedblleft{}or\textquotedblright{}.

You have met its first half already: \textbf{\te{లే}-} is the same root behind \te{లేదు}, \textquotedblleft{}there isn't\textquotedblright{}. \te{లేదా} is literally the \emph{or-else} of that root — \textquotedblleft{}failing that\textquotedblright{}.

\textbf{\te{టీ} \te{లేదా} \te{పాలు}?} — \textquotedblleft{}tea or milk?\textquotedblright{} That is the whole of an offered choice, and you can now make one.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
A choice you can put to somebody.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{lēdā}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{lēdā}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} offer a choice between two drinks you know, using \emph{lēdā}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{anukō}, then say \emph{lēdā}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \te{లేదా} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}or\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[enduku]{\te{ఎందుకు} (enduku) — why?}

\label{lesson:TE-C74-why}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{lēdā} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \te{ఎందుకు}}
\textbf{\te{ఎందుకు}} (\emph{enduku}) — \textquotedblleft{}why?\textquotedblright{}.

Another word off the \textbf{\te{ఎ}-} question row you already know: \te{ఎక్కడ} \textquotedblleft{}where\textquotedblright{}, \te{ఎవరు} \textquotedblleft{}who\textquotedblright{}, and now \te{ఎందుకు} \textquotedblleft{}why\textquotedblright{}. The row keeps its shape and you keep getting the words free.

It goes where its answer goes, not at the front: \textbf{\te{మీరు} \te{ఎందుకు} \te{వెళ్తారు}?} — \textquotedblleft{}why do you go?\textquotedblright{}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The question the next word answers.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{enduku}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{enduku}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} ask \emph{enduku} about something somebody just told you
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{aḍugu}, then say \emph{enduku}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \te{ఎందుకు} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}why?\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[endukaṇṭē]{\te{ఎందుకంటే} (endukaṇṭē) — because}

\label{lesson:TE-C74-because}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{enduku} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \te{ఎందుకంటే}}
\textbf{\te{ఎందుకంటే}} (\emph{endukaṇṭē}) — \textquotedblleft{}because\textquotedblright{}.

Look at it: it \emph{is} \te{ఎందుకు} with \textbf{\te{అంటే}} glued on — \textquotedblleft{}if you ask why\textquotedblright{}. Telugu answers the question by repeating it and then continuing, which is the gluing habit of your very first lesson doing real work.

\textbf{\te{నేను} \te{వెళ్తాను}, \te{ఎందుకంటే} \te{పని} \te{ఉంది}} — \textquotedblleft{}I'll go, because there is work.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the reason clause comes second}]
Telugu can put the reason first, as \textbf{\te{పని} \te{ఉంది} \te{కాబట్టి} \te{నేను} \te{వెళ్తాను}}. With \te{ఎందుకంటే} it goes second, after the thing being explained, exactly where English puts it. Use \te{ఎందుకంటే} while that ordering is still the one you think in.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
A reason, attached to the thing it explains.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{endukaṇṭē}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{endukaṇṭē}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} answer an \emph{enduku} question with \emph{endukaṇṭē} and one word you know
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{ganṭa}, then say \emph{endukaṇṭē}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \te{ఎందుకంటే} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}because\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
